question: Best fractional CRO for a PE-backed company?
body:
## Direct Answer

The best fractional CRO for a PE-backed company is a former operator who has already carried a private-equity revenue mandate through at least one hold period, understands the value-creation plan, and can move a portfolio company from founder-led selling to a repeatable, forecastable engine inside two to four quarters. Look for a pattern of measurable ARR acceleration, a bias for GTM instrumentation over motivational selling, and comfort reporting directly to a board and deal partners on a monthly cadence.

There is no single named individual who is universally "the best" — the right fractional Chief Revenue Officer is the one whose scars match your thesis, your check size, and the specific inflection your portfolio company is stuck at. A PE-backed company is not hiring a coach; it is buying a time-boxed intervention that has to survive due diligence, protect EBITDA, and set up a clean equity story for the next buyer. This essay lays out exactly how to evaluate, select, and structure that hire so the person you bring in actually earns their multiple.

## What makes a fractional CRO different when the owner is private equity?

A fractional CRO in a founder-owned business is often solving for growth and hope. In a PE-backed company the same title carries a fundamentally different contract. The sponsor has a written value-creation plan (VCP), a target return, and a clock — most buyout holds run three to five years, and the revenue leader is expected to deliver against a specific slice of that thesis, whether that is net revenue retention, new-logo velocity, pricing power, or channel expansion. The fractional executive is effectively an instrument of the deal team, not just a functional leader inside the company.

That changes what "best" means. The strongest candidates think in enterprise value, not just quota attainment. They can read a quality-of-earnings report, understand how revenue quality affects the exit multiple, and articulate which GTM moves protect EBITDA versus which ones burn it. They are fluent in the language of the board deck: pipeline coverage ratios, magic number, CAC payback, logo and gross-dollar retention, and the bridge from this year's plan to the model the sponsor underwrote. A fractional CRO who cannot connect a sales-capacity plan to the LBO model will always feel like an outsider to the deal partners — and will be the first line item cut when returns tighten.

The fractional structure itself also fits the PE rhythm unusually well. Many portfolio companies are too small to justify a full-time CRO comp package (base plus bonus plus equity often exceeding $500K in total when fully loaded), yet too broken to run without senior revenue leadership. A fractional arrangement — typically two to four days a week over six to twelve months — buys operator-grade judgment at a fraction of the carry, with a natural off-ramp once a permanent, cheaper VP of Sales can run the machine the fractional leader built. See how this maps to broader hiring economics in our note on [when to hire a fractional versus full-time revenue leader](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-vs-fulltime-cro).

## How do you actually evaluate a fractional CRO for a PE portfolio company?

Start with the deal, not the résumé. Before you interview anyone, write down the one or two revenue levers the sponsor is underwriting and the timeframe. If the thesis is "consolidate a fragmented market and cross-sell," you need a CRO who has built cross-sell motions and integrated acquired sales teams — not a pure new-logo hunter. If the thesis is "professionalize a founder-led sales org and install forecasting discipline," you need an operator, not a rainmaker. The single most common mis-hire in this category is pattern-matching on a big logo ("they were CRO at a unicorn") when the underlying motion is completely different from yours.

Then evaluate along five concrete dimensions. First, **hold-period evidence**: have they carried a number through a full PE cycle, and can they name the entry and exit metrics? Second, **diagnostic speed**: a strong fractional CRO delivers a written revenue diagnosis — pipeline health, team ranking, pricing leakage, forecast reliability — within the first 30 days, not a vague "listening tour." Third, **systems fluency**: they should be opinionated about CRM hygiene, forecasting cadence, and comp-plan design, because those are the durable assets that survive their departure. Fourth, **board credibility**: they can present bad news to deal partners without spin and defend a number under pressure. Fifth, **transition design**: the best ones plan their own obsolescence, hiring or elevating the permanent leader who inherits the engine.

The diagram below shows the evaluation flow most disciplined PE operating teams run, from thesis to signed engagement.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Write the revenue thesis and clock] --> B[Define the one or two levers]
    B --> C[Source operators who ran that exact motion]
    C --> D[Reference check on hold period outcomes]
    D --> E[30 day diagnostic as a paid trial]
    E --> F{Diagnosis credible and specific}
    F -->|Yes| G[Sign time boxed engagement with metrics]
    F -->|No| C
    G --> H[Plan the permanent handoff from day one]
```

Reference checks deserve special weight here. Ask former sponsors and CEOs three questions: did the number move, did they leave behind a system that outlived them, and would you rehire them at the next portfolio company. Vague warmth is a red flag; specific numbers and one honest weakness is the signal you want. For a deeper checklist, our guide on [reference-checking a revenue executive](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-exec-reference-checks) breaks down the exact questions and the answers that should worry you.

## What should the first 90 days look like?

The engagement lives or dies in the first quarter, and PE deal teams watch it closely because it signals whether the value-creation plan is on track. A credible fractional CRO front-loads diagnosis and instrumentation, resisting the temptation to "sell their way out" of structural problems. The pattern that repeatedly works is diagnose, stabilize, then build — in that order. Skipping straight to building (new comp plans, new territories, new tools) before diagnosing usually amplifies the existing dysfunction.

In the first 30 days the fractional CRO should produce a written revenue audit: a ranked assessment of every rep, an honest pipeline scrub that separates real opportunities from wishful ones, a forecast-accuracy baseline, and a pricing-leakage estimate. This document is gold to the sponsor because it converts anecdote into a plan. In days 30 to 60 the focus shifts to stabilization — fixing forecast cadence, tightening the deal-review discipline, and making one or two high-conviction personnel calls, because a weak rep tolerated for a full quarter costs the company real enterprise value. By days 60 to 90 the leader is building the durable machine: comp-plan redesign aligned to the VCP, a repeatable pipeline-generation motion, and the beginnings of the permanent-leadership plan.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Days 1 to 30 Diagnose] --> B[Days 31 to 60 Stabilize]
    B --> C[Days 61 to 90 Build]
    A --> A1[Written revenue audit]
    A --> A2[Rep ranking and pipeline scrub]
    B --> B1[Forecast cadence fixed]
    B --> B2[High conviction personnel calls]
    C --> C1[Comp plan aligned to plan]
    C --> C2[Permanent leader hiring plan]
```

A useful tell during this window is how the fractional CRO handles the forecast. Founder-led companies chronically over-forecast because optimism is rewarded. A strong operator will often lower the number in the first cycle, take the short-term board pain, and then beat a realistic figure — building the credibility that lets them run the rest of the plan. If a candidate promises to raise the forecast in month one without touching the underlying pipeline, that is theater, and the deal partners will eventually see through it. Our breakdown of [building a forecast the board actually trusts](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/board-trusted-forecast) covers the cadence and the coverage math in detail.

## How should you structure compensation and the engagement?

Compensation for a fractional CRO in a PE-backed company should mirror the sponsor's own incentive logic: mostly variable, tied to the value-creation plan, with a real equity or equity-like component so the leader is aligned to the exit rather than just the retainer. A common structure is a monthly retainer that reflects two to four days a week of committed time, plus a performance bonus tied to specific, pre-agreed metrics (net new ARR, retention, forecast accuracy), plus a slice of equity or a synthetic-equity/phantom arrangement that vests on outcomes. The exact figures vary widely by company size and geography, so treat any single number you see quoted online with suspicion — anchor instead on the principle of alignment to the VCP.

Be deliberate about scope and authority. The single biggest reason these engagements fail is ambiguity about whether the fractional leader can actually hire, fire, and change comp, or whether they are a highly paid advisor with no teeth. In a PE context, put decision rights in writing: does the CRO have hire/fire authority over the sales org, do they own the pricing model, do they present directly to the board. A fractional CRO with responsibility but no authority is set up to fail, and the sponsor will wrongly conclude the "revenue problem" was unfixable when it was really a governance problem.

Finally, structure the exit into the entry. The healthiest engagements name the end state on day one: the fractional CRO builds the machine and hires or elevates the permanent leader, then rolls off or shifts to a light advisory cadence. This protects the sponsor from becoming permanently dependent on a part-time executive and gives the fractional leader a clean, referenceable win. When the handoff is planned, the enterprise value the CRO built stays in the company after they leave — which is, ultimately, the entire point of the hire.

## Where do you find the best fractional CROs, and what are the red flags?

The strongest fractional CROs for PE-backed companies rarely come from job boards. They come from three channels: the sponsor's own operating-partner network, referrals from other portfolio-company CEOs, and specialist fractional-executive firms that vet operators specifically for private-equity mandates. Operating partners at mid-market and lower-middle-market funds usually keep a bench of proven revenue operators they redeploy across the portfolio — leaning on that bench is often faster and lower-risk than an open search. Specialist marketplaces and boutique firms have emerged precisely to serve this need, and they pre-screen for hold-period experience, though you still owe your own diagnostic and reference work.

Watch for a specific set of red flags. Be wary of the **perennial fractional** who has held eight three-month engagements in two years and never stayed long enough to be measured on an outcome — depth beats breadth here. Be wary of the **big-logo tourist** whose only credential is a title at a famous company operating a motion nothing like yours. Be wary of anyone who **won't commit to written metrics** or who bristles at board scrutiny, because PE governance is non-negotiable and their discomfort predicts friction. And be wary of the candidate who leads with **their playbook** rather than your diagnosis — a template applied before understanding your specific pipeline, pricing, and team is how good operators become bad hires. For a wider view of the market and how to run the search itself, our [fractional executive market overview](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-exec-market) is a useful companion read.

## Related questions

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A consultant advises and hands you a deck; a fractional CRO owns the number, carries decision authority over the sales org, and is accountable to the board for outcomes. In PE, you almost always want the operator, not the advisor.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run six to twelve months — long enough to diagnose, stabilize, and build a durable engine plus hire a permanent successor, but time-boxed so the portfolio company does not grow dependent on part-time senior leadership.

### Can a fractional CRO help prepare a company for exit?
Yes, and it is one of the highest-leverage uses. A strong fractional CRO cleans up revenue quality, tightens forecasting, and documents a repeatable motion — all of which raise revenue durability and, with it, the exit multiple during diligence.

### Should the fractional CRO report to the CEO or the sponsor?
Operationally to the CEO, but with a direct, transparent line to the board and deal partners. Attempting to hide the CRO from the sponsor, or routing them around the CEO, both create governance failures that sink the engagement.

### Is a fractional CRO cheaper than a full-time CRO?
Usually yes on cash terms, because you pay for two to four days a week instead of a fully loaded full-time package. But the real saving is optionality — you buy senior judgment for the inflection, then transition to a lower-cost permanent leader once the machine runs.

## FAQ

**What size company benefits most from a fractional CRO?**
Typically lower-middle-market and middle-market portfolio companies — roughly the stage where founder-led selling has plateaued and revenue is meaningful enough to warrant senior leadership, but not yet large enough to justify a full-time CRO comp package. The exact revenue band varies, but the tell is a company that has outgrown its founder's selling capacity and lacks forecasting discipline.

**How quickly should I expect results?**
Expect a credible written diagnosis within 30 days and visible operational improvements — cleaner forecast, tighter deal reviews, a personnel call or two — within 90 days. Meaningful revenue acceleration usually shows in two to four quarters, matching the natural sales cycle of most B2B portfolio companies.

**Does a fractional CRO need industry-specific experience?**
Motion fit matters more than vertical fit. A CRO who has run your exact GTM motion — say, mid-market SaaS with a two-call close — in an adjacent industry will usually outperform someone from your exact vertical who has only ever run a different motion. Prioritize how they sell over what they sold.

**Who manages the fractional CRO day to day?**
The CEO owns the operational relationship, while the sponsor's operating partner or deal team monitors outcomes through the board cadence. Clarity on this at the start prevents the common failure where the CRO gets conflicting direction from the CEO and the fund.

**What happens to the sales team when a fractional CRO arrives?**
Expect an early, honest rep ranking and one or two departures — a competent fractional CRO will not carry underperformers through a full quarter because the enterprise-value cost is too high. The best ones pair this with visible investment in the strong performers, so morale stabilizes rather than cratering.

**Can a fractional CRO become full-time?**
Sometimes, and it can be a clean outcome if the fit is strong and the company scales into the role. More often the healthiest path is the fractional leader building the engine and then hiring or elevating a permanent successor, with the fractional executive rolling to a light advisory cadence.

**How do I measure whether the engagement worked?**
Agree on three to five metrics up front tied to the value-creation plan — net new ARR, retention, forecast accuracy, pipeline coverage — and review them monthly. The durable test is whether the revenue engine keeps running after the fractional CRO leaves; if it collapses, you bought a dependency, not a system.
